key_facts: Very common **benign** epidermal tumour: waxy, warty, **'stuck-on'** papules and plaques, tan to black.
Over **90% of adults over 60** have at least one; usually start in the 30s–40s.
Not premalignant; caused by clonal mutations (e.g. **FGFR3, PIK3CA**) in keratinocytes, not sebum or viruses.
Dermoscopy: **milia-like cysts**, comedo-like openings, 'brain-like' ridges and sharp edges.
Reassure if typical; refer anything atypical (melanoma mimic). Sudden eruption of many SKs (**Leser–Trélat**) may signal internal malignancy.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Core SK content (definition, cause, sites, basic management) is in the [older skin pages](condition:itch-xerosis-older-adults) notes and is not repeated here.** This section adds dermoscopy, "the SK that changes", irritated SK and Leser–Trélat.
A benign epidermal tumour that is almost universal with age, often multiple, and the commonest "changing lesion" seen in primary care.
Eponymous signs often mixed up in exams.

sub: Extremely common in older adults of all ethnic groups; uncommon under 20.
Numbers increase with age; a strong family tendency in some people.
**Dermatosis papulosa nigra**: many small dark papules on the face and neck, especially in people of African or Asian descent.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Activating **FGFR3/PIK3CA** mutations in keratinocytes; it is a clonal benign neoplasm, not a pre-cancer. Lesions thicken, darken, catch on clothing, become **irritated/inflamed** and itch. That is exactly the "changing, itchy" story in [Case 3](condition:seborrhoeic-keratosis), and the same story fits melanoma.

ul: Clonal somatic mutations in **FGFR3, PIK3CA, RAS, AKT1, EGFR**.
Sun exposure may contribute (more on exposed sites); friction in body folds.
Eruptive SKs may follow inflammatory dermatoses or sunburn; **Leser–Trélat sign** with internal cancer is rare.
**"It's from greasy skin"**: the name is misleading; SKs are not related to sebum or sebaceous glands.
**"They are warts and spread"**: they are not viral or contagious.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: An SK is a **benign clonal overgrowth** of epidermal keratinocytes that sits on top of the skin.

mech.t: Keratinocytes acquire activating mutations (often FGFR3 or PIK3CA) that drive orderly but excessive growth.
The thickened epidermis grows **outwards above the skin surface**, so the lesion looks stuck on and can almost be lifted off.
mech.caption: A seborrhoeic keratosis sitting on the skin surface, with horn cysts within it.

mech.t: Keratin collects in small cysts (milia-like cysts on dermoscopy); melanin transferred from melanocytes darkens many lesions.
Friction or trauma can inflame an SK, making it red, crusted or bleeding, which can mimic cancer.

histo: Acanthosis of basaloid keratinocytes with **horn pseudocysts**, hyperkeratosis and papillomatosis; the base is flat (the 'string sign').
Variants: acanthotic, hyperkeratotic, reticulated, clonal, irritated. Biopsy if any doubt.

ul: "Stuck-on", waxy, verrucous, fissured papules and plaques, tan to black, on the trunk, face and scalp.
**Irritated SK:** red rim, crust and itch. This mimics SCC or melanoma.

**Sign of Leser–Trélat**: sudden eruption of many SKs (often with acanthosis nigricans or itch). It has been linked to internal malignancy (gastric/colorectal adenocarcinoma, lymphoma), but **the evidence is weak and contested**, because SKs are so common. Look for systemic symptoms rather than labelling everyone. Eruptive SKs also occur with **drugs** (e.g. cytarabine, docetaxel, BRAF inhibitors) and after inflammatory dermatoses (erythroderma).

head: Sign
Meaning
rows: **Periungual pigment spreading onto the proximal or lateral nail fold** from a longitudinal melanonychia. This suggests **subungual (acral) melanoma**. Cross-reference the [nail disorders](condition:paronychia) notes (melanonychia) and the [melanoma](condition:melanoma) notes
Pigment visible through a transparent cuticle (benign naevus, ethnic pigmentation, Laugier–Hunziker, drugs such as zidovudine, minocycline, hydroxyurea, chemotherapy)
Vesicles on the **tip/side of the nose** (nasociliary branch of V1) predict ophthalmic involvement, so same-day ophthalmology
Congenital syphilis: notched incisors, interstitial keratitis, deafness
Short 4th/5th metacarpals ("knuckle-knuckle-dimple-dimple" when making a fist); osteoma cutis
Large unilateral **"coast of Maine"** café-au-lait macules (jagged), polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, precocious puberty (GNAS mosaicism). NF1 CALMs are smooth, like the "coast of California"

sub: Dermatosis papulosa nigra is common and benign; treat only for cosmetic reasons, with care to avoid pigment change.

ul: **Milia-like cysts** (white/yellow "stars" or round bodies)
**Comedo-like openings** (keratin-filled crypts)
**Fissures and ridges** ("brain-like"/cerebriform, "fat fingers")
**Sharp, "moth-eaten" border**
**Hairpin vessels** with a white halo, in irritated or thick lesions

**Caveat:** some SKs show multiple colours or blue-black areas, and **"collision" lesions** (SK beside a melanoma or BCC) exist. **Melanoma can mimic SK**, especially in men's backs, like [Case 3](condition:seborrhoeic-keratosis) sailor.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses

ddx.name: Melanoma
ddx.f: Evolving asymmetry, atypical network, blue-white veil; no cysts or openings.

blocks: A **single nail band that is new, widening (>3 mm), dark, irregular, or in an adult aged over 50, especially of the thumb or great toe, or with Hutchinson's sign** needs urgent dermatology (suspected cancer pathway). Skin of colour often has *multiple* benign bands. A *single* changing band is the concern.

sections.title: Management

ul: **Apply the NICE NG12 weighted 7-point checklist to any changing lesion:** Major features (2 points each): change in size, irregular shape, irregular colour; Minor features (1 point each): largest diameter ≥7 mm, inflammation, oozing, change in sensation (e.g. itch); [Case 3](condition:seborrhoeic-keratosis): "changing" (2) + **itchy** (1) = **3 → suspected cancer pathway**. This is unless the lesion is confidently a classic SK on dermoscopy by a trained clinician (see *Where course teaching differs from UK guidance*)
Even when the score is below 3, refer if there is **any** doubt. NG12 1.7.2 says dermoscopy suggesting melanoma means a suspected cancer referral.
**Confident SK:** reassure; leaflet. Itch: emollient ± a short course of a mild/moderate topical steroid for irritation.

Removal for cosmetic reasons is usually **not NHS-funded**. Cryotherapy, curettage or shave are used where symptomatic, with histology for curettage/shave if any doubt. **Never destroy (cryo) a lesion that might be melanoma.**
Topical **hydrogen peroxide 40%** (licensed in the US, not marketed in the UK) and other cosmetic options are not IP options.

blocks: Do not label nail pigmentation as fungal or traumatic without evidence. Haematomas grow out distally (mark the nail and re-check in 4–6 weeks), whereas melanoma bands remain at the matrix. Refer on the suspected cancer pathway when Hutchinson's sign is present.

blocks.h: Case 1: 50-year-old Asian woman, 5 mm pigmented arm papule, slow growth over 5 years

ul: **Diagnosis:** (pigmented) dermatofibroma.
**Bedside sign:** dimple / Fitzpatrick (pinch) sign. Dermoscopy: peripheral network with a central white patch.
**Immunostain:** **Factor XIIIa positive** (CD34 negative). DFSP is the reverse.
**IP plan:** reassure if classic. Refer if dermoscopy is atypical or the 7-point score is ≥3 (growth = 2 points, so one more feature tips it).

blocks.h: Case 2: 68-year-old woman, tender scaly 7×8 mm pinna nodule, post-stroke, losartan/aspirin/simvastatin

ul: **Bedside test:** gentle squeeze, which causes disproportionate tenderness. Also ask about the sleeping side.
**Diagnosis:** chondrodermatitis nodularis helicis.
**First-line treatment:** **pressure relief** (CNH foam protector/pillow with a hole; avoid sleeping on that side).
**Second-line:** intralesional or potent topical steroid, topical GTN (off-label), cryotherapy, cartilage excision.
**Biopsy if:** not resolving after 6–8 weeks of offloading, atypical features, or SCC/BCC suspected (NG12 1.7.4/1.7.5).
Do **not** stop aspirin for a biopsy.

blocks.h: Case 3: 55-year-old sailor, itchy back lesion changing over 6 months

ul: **Bedside test:** dermoscopy. Milia-like cysts, comedo-like openings, fissures/ridges, sharp border, and hairpin vessels mean SK.
**Diagnosis:** seborrhoeic keratosis. **Management:** reassure and discharge.

**UK IP version:** NG12 7-point score = change (2) + itch/sensation change (1) = **3**, which means the suspected cancer pathway *unless* a trained clinician has confidently made the dermoscopic SK diagnosis. An IP without dermoscopy competence should **refer**, not discharge. Also give sun-safety advice and a full skin check.
**Clear cell acanthoma:** red, moist, collarette-rimmed leg papule; **string-of-pearls** vessels on dermoscopy.
Reassure when typical. Cryotherapy or curettage only if symptomatic or diagnostic doubt; usually private/cosmetic on the NHS unless catching or bleeding.
Ugly-duckling or atypical → refer, do not freeze.

ladder.t: Reassure; leaflet; itch: emollient ± short mild steroid.
Score ≥ 3, dermoscopy suggesting melanoma (NG12 1.7.2), or **any doubt**: refer.
Cryo / curettage only if symptomatic (catching, bleeding, inflamed); cosmetic removal usually not NHS-funded.

refer.t: An ‘SK’ that is changing, has atypical dermoscopy, or stands out from the patient’s other SKs: **possible melanoma**.
Sudden eruption of many SKs with itch: consider internal malignancy (**Leser–Trélat**).

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: An ‘SK’ that is changing, has atypical dermoscopy or stands out from the patient’s other SKs: refer as a **possible melanoma**.
Sudden eruption of many SKs with itch: consider internal malignancy (**Leser–Trélat**).
Irritation, itch, catching on clothing and bleeding.
**Misdiagnosis**: melanoma, pigmented BCC or SCC can look like an SK.
Collision tumours (a cancer arising next to an SK) are rare.
Benign and permanent; new lesions keep appearing with age.
Removal (cryotherapy, curettage, shave) is usually cosmetic and not funded on the NHS unless symptomatic.

pearls: [Case 3](condition:seborrhoeic-keratosis) sailor has lifelong UV exposure, so he is at higher risk for melanoma, BCC and SCC. Give sun-protection advice and do a **full skin check** (other lesions, scalp, ears).
Teach the "ugly duckling" concept and ask about change using photos (patients can photograph lesions monthly).
Ask about drugs that cause melanonychia (hydroxycarbamide, zidovudine, minocycline, antimalarials, cytotoxics). Multiple nails and a matching start date make it drug-related.
